Content:
Suppose that we wish to calculate the limit

Content:
[MATH: L=\lim\limits_{h\to 0} \dfrac{\ln(2+h) -\ln(2)}{h}.]

Content:
The key here is to notice that the limit looks very similar to the instantaneous rate of change formula,
[MATH: f'(a) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0} \dfrac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},]
for the function [MATH: f(x) = \ln x] at [MATH: a=2.]

Content:
Let's substitute [MATH: f(x) = \ln x] and [MATH: a=2] into the above, just to be sure:

Content:
[MATH: f^{′}(2)|= lim_(h → 0)(f(2 + h) − f(2))/(h); = lim_(h → 0)(\ln (2 + h) − \ln (2))/(h); = L.]

Content:
This confirms that [MATH: L = f'(2).] So instead of working out that difficult limit, we only need to work out [MATH: f'(2).]

Content:
Computing the derivative, we have
[MATH: f'(x) = \frac{1}{x}, \qquad f'(2) = \dfrac{1}{2},]
and therefore we conclude that [MATH: L=\dfrac{1}{2}.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we let [MATH: L = \lim_{x\to\pi/3}\dfrac{\left(\sin(x) - \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}\right)}{\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)}.]

Comparing this with the formula for the instantaneous rate of change, [MATH: f'(a) = \dfrac{f(x) - f(a)}{x-a},]

we see that if we let [MATH: f(x) = \sin(x)] and [MATH: a=\dfrac{\pi}{3},] we get [MATH: f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \lim_{x\to a}\dfrac{\sin(x) - \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)}{\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)} =\lim_{x\to\pi/3}\dfrac{\left(\sin(x) - \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}\right)}{\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)}= L] This confirms that [MATH: L = f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right).]

Computing the derivative, we have [MATH: f'(x) = \cos(x), \qquad f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \cos{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)} = \dfrac{1}{2},] and therefore we conclude that [MATH: L=\dfrac 1 2.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that we wish to calculate the limit

Content:
[MATH: L=\lim\limits_{h\to 0} \dfrac{\ln(2+h) -\ln(2)}{h}.]

Content:
The key here is to notice that the limit looks very similar to the instantaneous rate of change formula,
[MATH: f'(a) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0} \dfrac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},]
for the function [MATH: f(x) = \ln x] at [MATH: a=2.]

Content:
Let's substitute [MATH: f(x) = \ln x] and [MATH: a=2] into the above, just to be sure:

Content:
[MATH: f^{′}(2)|= lim_(h → 0)(f(2 + h) − f(2))/(h); = lim_(h → 0)(\ln (2 + h) − \ln (2))/(h); = L.]

Content:
This confirms that [MATH: L = f'(2).] So instead of working out that difficult limit, we only need to work out [MATH: f'(2).]

Content:
Computing the derivative, we have
[MATH: f'(x) = \frac{1}{x}, \qquad f'(2) = \dfrac{1}{2},]
and therefore we conclude that [MATH: L=\dfrac{1}{2}.]

This confirms that [MATH: L=f'(3).]
